# P6 · IJB: Remote Sensing Without Code {#sec-p6-ijb .unnumbered}

::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
You will learn to use IJB, an Earth Engine application built by the author, to answer real questions (where did it flood, what burned, how has land cover changed, where is landslide risk highest) by clicking instead of coding. Everything P1 to P5 explained runs inside it: Sentinel-1 radar, Sentinel-2 composites, terrain, GEDI, machine learning. The rest of the book shows the code behind the same ideas; this chapter shows what you can do before writing a single line.
:::

## Why an app

Most people who need a flood map are not programmers: a disaster officer, a district planner, a student on the first day. For them a script is a wall. IJB (from *Indraja Buana*, "remote sensing of the earth") puts the most useful analyses of this book behind buttons, with sensible defaults chosen from the author's own projects. It gives beginners real results on day one, and gives experts a fast first look before they open the Code Editor.

What you still need is the understanding from P1 to P5. The app will happily produce a flood map from the wrong dates or a land-cover map from three badly placed samples. Knowing *why* radar sees water and *what* an accuracy number means is what separates a usable result from a pretty one.

## Opening IJB

IJB runs inside the Google Earth Engine Code Editor (Chapter [-@sec-ecosystem] explains how to get an account).

1. Sign in to Earth Engine, then open the repository link: <https://code.earthengine.google.com/?accept_repo=users/rifkynauvalhsp/IndrajaBuana>. The repository `IndrajaBuana` appears under *Reader* in the Scripts panel on the left.
2. Open the script called **app** in that repository.
3. Press **Run**. The Code Editor's map is replaced by the IJB screen.

The app loads only its frame at first. Each module is built the moment you press its button, so the app stays light, and if one module ever fails, its name and error appear on screen while the others keep working.

## The screen

## The app speaks Bahasa Indonesia
IJB's screen is in Bahasa Indonesia for now; an English interface is planned. This guide names every button exactly as it appears, in *italics*, with its English meaning in brackets the first time, for example *Jalankan analisis* (Run analysis).
:::

![The IJB screen: area, reporting unit and module on the left, the map on the right.](images/real/p6-layout-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="The IJB screen: area, reporting unit and module on the left, the map on the right."}

| Your question | Module | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| I need a basic layer (rainfall, buildings, peat, population...) for my area | **Data** | 43 public datasets in 13 groups, statistics per reporting unit |
| I need a clean satellite image without clouds | **Citra** | five ways to build a Sentinel-2 composite, band combinations and indices |
| What is the land cover here, by my own classes? | **Tutupan** | mark examples, choose an algorithm, get a map with accuracy and areas |
| I want a ready-made land-cover map or a canopy height map | **Model** | the author's 10-class model, Dynamic World, or canopy height trained on GEDI |
| When did this place change, or how old is this plantation? | **Deret** | harmonics, LandTrendr, stand age, CCDC breakpoints |
| What changed between two dates? | **Ubah** | index difference, Dynamic World transitions, double classification, trend |
| Where did it flood, and who was affected? | **Banjir** | Sentinel-1 change with Otsu threshold, HAND, slope and permanent-water filters; people and buildings |
| What burned, how badly, and on peat? | **Api** | dNBR in four severity classes, hotspots, burned peat and its thickness |
| Where is landslide or flood risk highest? | **Rawan** | random forest on embeddings and terrain, from your points or the NASA landslide catalog |
| I need to combine steps: threshold, clean up, vectorise, summarise | **Toolbox** | expression calculator, Otsu, raster ↔ vector, zonal statistics, SNIC, morphology |

: Which module to open for which question.

The left panel walks you through three steps. The map on the right shows your area, every result layer, a legend and a status bar telling you what the app is doing.

### Step 1: area of interest

Every analysis needs an area. There are four ways to set it:

- **Draw** (*Gambar*) a rectangle (*Kotak*) or polygon (*Poligon*) on the map.
- **Choose an administrative unit** (*Wilayah*): *Pilih provinsi*, then *Pilih kabupaten atau kota*, from the official boundaries.
- **Paste** (*Tempel*) a geometry copied from QGIS, or four numbers of a bounding box (west, south, east, north).
- **Load a public Earth Engine asset** (*Aset*, then *Muat aset*), for example a boundary you uploaded yourself.

The app checks the size first and rejects areas over 25,000 km², because larger analyses would run out of time. A regency is usually well within the limit; a whole province often is not.

### Step 2: reporting unit

Choose whether statistics and tables are summarised per **province, regency, subdistrict (kecamatan) or village (desa)**. Subdistricts and villages use the community geoBoundaries dataset. A flood map summarised per village is what an emergency response actually needs.

### Step 3: choose a module

Ten buttons, ten kinds of question. The table above says which to open for what. The sections below explain each, with the settings that matter.

## The modules

In every module below, the first picture is the screen with **the buttons to press outlined in red and numbered in order**. The pictures after it are real results made in this book with the same method the button runs, so you know what to expect; in the app they appear over your own area.

### Data: the catalogue

![IJB Data: before pressing (left, red buttons in order) and after (right).](images/real/p6-click-data-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Data: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Wilayah* (Region): choose province and regency · ② *Data* · ③ *Kelompok* (Group): *Curah hujan* · ④ *Lapisan* (Layer) · ⑤ *Rentang tanggal* (Date range) · ⑥ *Tampilkan lapisan* (Show layer)

**After you press:** the result cards show *rerata di AOI* (mean over the area) and *jenis* (type); the map shows the result layer.


Forty-three ready datasets in thirteen groups: hydrology, rainfall, terrain, land cover, buildings and population, fire and peat, drought, coasts and ecosystems, soils, volcanoes, administrative boundaries, event history and machine learning. Examples: CHIRPS and GPM rainfall, HAND and MERIT Hydro, four elevation models (FABDEM, Copernicus GLO-30, NASADEM, SRTM), Dynamic World and WorldCover, Google, Microsoft and VIDA building footprints, WorldPop and GHSL population, FIRMS hotspots, burned area, peat extent and peat thickness, mangroves, SMAP soil moisture, the NASA global landslide catalogue and the satellite embeddings. Pick a group and a layer, set a date range where relevant, and press *Tampilkan lapisan*: the layer appears on the map with its mean over your area.

**Use it for:** a first look at any place, and background layers before any analysis.

**What you get**

![Annual rainfall, the kind of layer Data shows (Chapter [-@sec-dataviz]).](images/real/ch29-map-sequential.jpg){.lightbox fig-alt="Annual rainfall, the kind of layer Data shows."}

### Citra: a clean Sentinel-2 image

![IJB Citra: before pressing (left, red buttons in order) and after (right).](images/real/p6-click-citra-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Citra: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Wilayah* · ② *Citra* · ③ *Metode komposit* (Composite method): *Cloud Score Plus (terbaik)* · ④ *Rentang tanggal* (Date range) · ⑤ *Kombinasi band* (Band combination) · ⑥ *Susun komposit* (Build composite)

**After you press:** the result cards show *citra tersedia* (images available) and *piksel bersih* (clear pixels); the map shows the result layer.


Builds a cloud-free composite from all Sentinel-2 images in a date range, not one scene. Five methods: **Cloud Score Plus** (the default and usually the best in the tropics), median with the scene classification mask, greenest pixel, 25th percentile (bright, low-haze) and the single cleanest scene. You set the date range, the maximum cloud per scene, the Cloud Score Plus threshold, the band combination (natural colour, vegetation infrared, urban SWIR, agriculture, or haze penetration) and optionally an index (NDVI, NDWI, NDBI, NBR or NDMI). The app reports how many images were used and how many pixels came out clean. (P1 and Chapter [-@sec-cloud] explain why these choices matter.)

**What you get**

![A cloud-free median composite, what Citra builds (Chapter [-@sec-cloud]).](images/real/ch09-truecolour.jpg){.lightbox fig-alt="A cloud-free median composite, what Citra builds."}

### Tutupan: your own land-cover map

![IJB Tutupan: before pressing (left, red buttons in order) and after (right).](images/real/p6-click-tutupan-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Tutupan: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Wilayah* · ② *Tutupan* · ③ *Sumber data* (Data source) · ④ *Algoritma* (Algorithm): *Random Forest* · ⑤ *Tambah* (Add) a class · ⑥ *Tandai* (Mark), then click examples on the map · ⑦ *Latih dan klasifikasi* (Train and classify)

**After you press:** the result cards show *akurasi keseluruhan* (overall accuracy) and *kappa*, with the area of every class; the map shows the result layer.


The supervised classification of Chapter [-@sec-supervised], by clicking:

1. Choose the data source (Sentinel-2 composite, Sentinel-1, satellite embeddings, terrain or Dynamic World) and the date range.
2. **Add your classes** (*Tambah*): for example forest, rice field, settlement, water.
3. For each class, press *Tandai* and click examples on the map.
4. Choose the algorithm: Random Forest (recommended), Gradient Tree Boost, SVM, CART, Minimum Distance, or K-Means if you want clusters without samples.
5. Set the minimum mapping unit to remove speckled single pixels, then press *Latih dan klasifikasi*.

The app reports **overall accuracy and kappa** and the area of every class. Remember Chapter [-@sec-accuracy]: accuracy on points you clicked yourself near each other is optimistic. Spread your samples over the whole area.

**What you get**

![A random-forest land-cover map, what Tutupan returns (Chapter [-@sec-supervised]).](images/real/ch16-rf.jpg){.lightbox fig-alt="A random-forest land-cover map, what Tutupan returns."}

### Model: ready-made models, including the author's own

![IJB Model: before pressing (left, red buttons in order) and after (right).](images/real/p6-click-model-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Model: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Wilayah* · ② *Model* · ③ *Mode*: *Model 10 kelas milik sendiri*, *Dynamic World* or *Tinggi tajuk dari GEDI* (canopy height from GEDI) · ④ *Tahun embedding* (Embedding year) · ⑤ *Jalankan model* (Run model)

**After you press:** the result cards show *kelas dominan* (dominant class), *luas kelas dominan* (its area), *korelasi GEDI* (correlation with GEDI) and *tinggi rerata* (mean height); the map shows the result layer.


Three modes:

- **The author's 10-class model**: a classifier trained on satellite embeddings, elevation and slope, mapping plantation, forest, agriculture, open land, water, mangrove, rice field, oil palm, sago and rubber. Choose the embedding year (2021–2025) and press run. No samples needed; the model was trained in advance and is applied to your area.
- **Dynamic World**: Google's near-real-time land cover, for comparison.
- **Canopy height from GEDI**: the app takes GEDI laser heights in your area (good-quality shots only), trains a regression on the embeddings, and predicts a wall-to-wall 10 m canopy height map. It reports the correlation with the GEDI shots and the mean height (Chapters [-@sec-height-scaling] and [-@sec-gedi-structure]).

**What you get**

![Land cover from satellite embeddings with few samples, the idea behind the ready-made model (Chapter [-@sec-embeddings]).](images/real/ch19-classified.jpg){.lightbox fig-alt="Land cover from satellite embeddings with few samples, the idea behind the ready-made model."}

![A 10 m canopy height map trained on GEDI, the kind of result the height mode gives (Chapter [-@sec-height-scaling]).](images/real/ch33-eth-map.jpg){.lightbox fig-alt="A 10 m canopy height map trained on GEDI, the kind of result the height mode gives."}

### Deret: time series

![IJB Deret: before pressing (left, red buttons in order) and after (right).](images/real/p6-click-deret-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Deret: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Wilayah* · ② *Deret* · ③ *Mode*: *Harmonik dan tren*, *Titik patah LandTrendr* or *Umur tegakan atau tanaman* (stand or crop age) · ④ *Rentang tahun* (Year range) · ⑤ *Jalankan analisis* (Run analysis)

**After you press:** the result cards show *tahun gangguan dominan* (main disturbance year), *luas terganggu* (area disturbed), *umur rerata* (mean age) and *amplitudo musiman* (seasonal amplitude); the map shows the result layer.


For when something happened and how long ago (Chapters [-@sec-timeseries] and [-@sec-oil-palm-age]). Four modes: **harmonic model and trend** (separates the season from the long-term trend, reports the seasonal amplitude), **LandTrendr breakpoints** (the year of the main disturbance), **stand or crop age**, and **CCDC breakpoints** (precise break dates, slower). Set the year range, the number of harmonics and the change-magnitude threshold.

**What you get**

![Plantation age from the year of disturbance, what Deret's age mode maps (Chapter [-@sec-oil-palm-age]).](images/real/ch44-age.jpg){.lightbox fig-alt="Plantation age from the year of disturbance, what Deret's age mode maps."}

### Ubah: change between two dates

![IJB Ubah: before pressing (left, red buttons in order) and after (right).](images/real/p6-click-ubah-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Ubah: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Wilayah* · ② *Ubah* · ③ *Metode* (Method): *Selisih indeks*, *Transisi Dynamic World* or *Klasifikasi ganda* · ④ *Periode pertama* and *Periode kedua* (first and second period) · ⑤ *Jalankan deteksi* (Run detection)

**After you press:** the result cards show *hektar bertambah* (hectares gained) and *hektar berkurang* (hectares lost); the map shows the result layer.


Four methods: **index difference** (NDVI, NDWI, NDBI, NBR or NDMI between two periods, with a threshold), **Dynamic World transitions**, **double classification**, and **linear trend**. It reports hectares gained and lost. For the exact date of a change, use Deret instead.

**What you get**

![New built-up land between two years from Dynamic World (Chapter [-@sec-timeseries]).](images/real/ch21-new-built.jpg){.lightbox fig-alt="New built-up land between two years from Dynamic World."}

![The same change as a chart, year by year.](images/real/ch21-built-series.png){.lightbox fig-alt="The same change as a chart, year by year."}

### Banjir: flood mapping

![IJB Banjir: before pressing (left, red buttons in order) and after (right).](images/real/p6-click-banjir-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Banjir: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Wilayah*: your regency · ② *Satuan Pelaporan* (Reporting unit): *Desa* (village) · ③ *Banjir* · ④ *Periode sebelum kejadian* and *Periode saat atau sesudah* (before, and during or after) · ⑤ *Arah orbit* (Orbit direction) · ⑥ *Batas HAND* (HAND limit) · ⑦ *Jalankan analisis* (Run analysis)

**After you press:** the result cards show *hektar tergenang* (hectares flooded), *jiwa terpapar* (people exposed), *bangunan* (buildings) and *cocok riwayat* (match with the flood record); the map shows the result layer.


The method of Chapter [-@sec-flood] and P5, by clicking:

1. Set a **period before** the flood and a **period during or after** it.
2. Choose the **orbit direction** (descending or ascending; pick the one that passed during your event).
3. Choose the **elevation model** (FABDEM by default, with trees and buildings removed) and the **HAND limit**, the height above the nearest drainage beyond which water is not plausible (15 m by default).
4. Press *Jalankan analisis*.

Behind the button: Sentinel-1 backscatter change, an automatic Otsu threshold, then filters for steep slopes, permanent water and high HAND. The results are **hectares flooded, people exposed, buildings affected** and how well the flood matches the historical flood record. Summarised by your reporting unit, that is a first situation report.

**What you get**

![Radar flood extent with Otsu threshold and HAND, the method behind Banjir (Chapter [-@sec-flood]).](images/real/ch24-flood-map.jpg){.lightbox fig-alt="Radar flood extent with Otsu threshold and HAND, the method behind Banjir."}

![The HAND check: flooded points sit low on the terrain.](images/real/ch24-flood-hand.png){.lightbox fig-alt="The HAND check: flooded points sit low on the terrain."}

### Api: forest and land fire

![IJB Api: before pressing (left, red buttons in order) and after (right).](images/real/p6-click-api-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Api: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Wilayah* · ② *Api* · ③ *Periode sebelum* and *Periode sesudah* (before and after) · ④ *Jalankan analisis* (Run analysis)

**After you press:** the result cards show *hektar terbakar* (hectares burned), *titik panas* (hotspots), *hektar gambut* (hectares of peat burned) and *tebal gambut rerata* (mean peat thickness); the map shows the result layer.


1. Set a **period before** and a **period after** the fire season.
2. Press *Jalankan analisis*.

The app computes the difference in Normalised Burn Ratio (dNBR) from Sentinel-2 and splits it into four severity classes, with breaks at dNBR 0.27, 0.44 and 0.66. It overlays FIRMS hotspots and the peat map, and reports **hectares burned, hotspots, hectares of burned peat and the mean peat thickness**. A hectare of burned peat is not a hectare of burned grass (Chapters [-@sec-peat] and [-@sec-carbon-balance]).

**What you get**

![Burned area on peat in 2015, the result Api reports with burned peat (Chapter [-@sec-peat]).](images/real/ch37-burn-2015.jpg){.lightbox fig-alt="Burned area on peat in 2015, the result Api reports with burned peat."}

![Hotspots against rainfall, the chart behind the fire numbers.](images/real/ch37-series.png){.lightbox fig-alt="Hotspots against rainfall, the chart behind the fire numbers."}

### Rawan: hazard susceptibility with machine learning

![IJB Rawan: before pressing (left, red buttons in order) and after (right).](images/real/p6-click-rawan-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Rawan: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Wilayah* · ② *Rawan* · ③ *Jenis bahaya* (Hazard type): *Longsor* (landslide) · ④ *Tandai RAWAN* (mark hazardous), click places · ⑤ *Tandai AMAN* (mark safe), click places · ⑥ *Latih dari titik manual* (Train from manual points)

**After you press:** the result cards show *akurasi validasi* (validation accuracy), *kappa*, *hektar rawan tinggi* (hectares of high susceptibility) and *jiwa di zona rawan* (people in high-susceptibility zones); the map shows the result layer.


Maps where landslides or floods are *likely*, not where they happened. A random forest learns from the 64 satellite embedding bands plus slope, elevation, aspect, TWI, HAND, rainfall, soil and land cover.

1. Choose the **hazard** (landslide, flood, or general), the **embedding year** and the **elevation model**.
2. Give it examples, in one of two ways:
   - **Automatically**, from the NASA global landslide catalogue (*Latih otomatis*), or
   - **By hand**: press *Tandai RAWAN* and click places known to be hazardous, then *Tandai AMAN* and click safe places, then *Latih dari titik manual*.
3. Set the number of trees (120 by default).

It reports **validation accuracy, kappa, hectares of high susceptibility and people living in high-susceptibility zones**. Hand-placed points from people who know the area usually beat a global catalogue.

**What you get**

![A landslide susceptibility map (Chapter [-@sec-landslide-simple]); Rawan learns the weights with a random forest instead of fixing them.](images/real/ch50-score.jpg){.lightbox fig-alt="A landslide susceptibility map; Rawan learns the weights with a random forest instead of fixing them."}

### Toolbox: chain your own workflow

Every result becomes the **active layer**, and every tool works on the active layer, so tools can be chained (figure below). The tools: an **expression calculator** for any band formula, **Otsu threshold**, **raster to vector** (with minimum mapping unit and line simplification), **vector to raster** (buildings, landslides, mangroves or your last vector), **zonal statistics** (mean, sum, maximum, minimum, mode, standard deviation, median), **SNIC object segmentation** (Chapter [-@sec-obia]) and **morphological filters and sieve**.

![Chaining tools: every result becomes the active layer for the next one.](images/real/p6-chain-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="Chaining tools: every result becomes the active layer for the next one."}

## Four recipes

**A flood situation report.** Step 1: choose the regency. Step 2: reporting unit *Desa*. Banjir: before period a month before the event, after period the days just after it, the orbit that passed during the flood. Run. Read hectares, people and buildings per village; check the map against news photographs before sharing it.

**A burn-severity map for a peat district.** Api with a before period in June–July and an after period in October–November of a dry year. Read the burned peat and its thickness; use Data → FIRMS to compare with hotspot counts.

**Urban growth.** Ubah with *Dynamic World transitions* between two years, or *Selisih indeks* on NDBI. For building counts, Data → VIDA building footprints, then Toolbox → zonal statistics per village.

**A quick land-cover map with no samples.** Model → the 10-class model for the latest embedding year. If your area has classes the model never saw, switch to Tutupan and train your own.

## Using an app responsibly

- **Dates are everything.** A flood map from the wrong week maps rice-field irrigation (Chapter [-@sec-paddy]).
- **Read the numbers the app gives you,** especially accuracy and kappa, and treat any map without them as a draft.
- **Check against something independent**: field reports, high-resolution basemaps, news photographs.
- **Credit the data.** Every layer in the catalogue has an owner; name them when you publish a map.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Map a flood you know (for example in your own district) with Banjir. Which orbit direction passed closest to the event date?
2. Train Tutupan twice for the same area: once with five samples per class clustered in one corner, once with twenty spread out. Compare the accuracy and the maps.
3. Run Model → canopy height for a forest area. Where does the GEDI-trained map disagree most with your expectations?
4. Use Rawan with manual points in a landslide-prone valley you know. How many points does it take before the map stops changing?
